author.name: HCMC Insider
author.about: A local in Ho Chi Minh City who eats, walks and photographs the city, mostly around Cholon.

stories.title: Hỷ Ký: chicken noodles with xá kén in Phú Bình
stories.dek: A morning-only chicken noodle shop in a Phú Bình alley, where the dipping bowl of xá kén is the real star. 50,000 dong a bowl.

photos.alt: Two bowls of chicken noodle soup with bean sprouts, a steel bowl of chopped xá kén and dipping sauces on a steel table
photos.caption: The full spread at Hỷ Ký: chicken noodles, bean sprouts, xá kén and dipping sauces.

photos.alt: A piece of boiled chicken with yellow, finely dimpled skin held up with chopsticks over egg noodles
photos.caption: Yellow, dimpled skin over a thin ivory layer.

photos.alt: Chicken pieces in a clear golden broth with spring onion
photos.caption: Clear, golden broth, chicken on top, noodles and sprouts underneath.

photos.alt: A steel bowl of chopped xá kén next to small bowls of dipping sauce with chilli and green chilli slices
photos.caption: Help yourself: the xá kén bowl on the table, then chilli sauce, green chilli and the dark dipping sauce.

photos.alt: A bowl of egg noodles in broth with boiled chicken and chopped xá kén on top
photos.caption: A normal bowl, 50,000 dong.

photos.alt: Boiled chicken pieces in broth topped with spring onion
photos.caption: Chicken served in broth on the side.

photos.alt: Egg noodles in broth topped with chopped xá kén, chopsticks and spoon
photos.caption: Noodles with a spoonful of xá kén stirred in.

photos.alt: Plain egg noodles in clear broth with spring onion and a side of bean sprouts
photos.caption: Yellow egg noodles in clear broth.

body: I ate at Mì gà Hỷ Ký, a long-running shop in the Phú Bình parish area of old District 11. A normal bowl of chicken noodles with xá kén costs 50,000 dong.

The bowl arrives neat: a clear, golden broth, finely chopped spring onion, yellow egg noodles and bean sprouts at the bottom. Lift the chicken and the skin is yellow with tiny dimples, over a thin ivory layer. The meat is tender and fragrant, and even before any sauce you can clearly taste the chicken.

Then comes the dipping bowl. Chopped xá kén sits in a whole steel bowl on the table; you spoon some into your own dish, add chilli sauce, a few slices of green chilli and a splash of the dark brown dipping sauce. Dip the chicken in and it is hot and pungent, nothing like the ginger fish sauce or salt, pepper and lime I usually have with boiled chicken. Eat it once and you remember it; it doesn't taste like anything else.
From what I've read, xá kén is a kind of root and is considered the soul of this dish. And yellow, dimpled skin like this, as far as I know, usually means a free-range local chicken (gà ta).

The Phú Bình housing area is said to be the capital of chicken noodles with xá kén. Going there myself, I counted about five or six shops. I've eaten at quite a few, and Hỷ Ký is still the one I think is most worth it.
Beyond the taste, the shop is very clean. The young owner has a great memory: he takes orders without writing anything down and works fast.
The downside is seating. The shop is in a narrow alley; come late and it's full, with no tables and a long wait. It sells in the morning and usually runs out by around 11 am, so go early.

You can also order a quarter or half chicken, and choose thigh, wing, back, upper thigh, feet or neck. Try a bite of chicken without sauce first to taste the bird, then move on to the xá kén. If you can't take much heat, go easy on it.
Verdict: worth the money, as long as you're willing to get up early. What do you usually dip boiled chicken in?

Practical info: Mì gà Hỷ Ký, 8L Lạc Long Quân, Hòa Bình ward (the Phú Bình area of old District 11), Ho Chi Minh City. 50,000 dong per normal bowl; quarter and half chickens available. Mornings only, usually sold out by about 11 am.

stories.title: Bún bò Phú Bình: a gentle bowl of Hue beef noodles
stories.dek: A morning-only Hue-style beef noodle shop in Phú Bình with a clean, sweet, spicy broth that is easy on first-timers. 50,000 dong a bowl.

photos.alt: A bowl of bún bò Huế with beef bone, chilli slices and chilli oil, with a plate of shredded greens and bean sprouts
photos.caption: A bowl at Bún bò Phú Bình, with the shredded greens and bean sprouts on the side.

photos.alt: A bowl of beef noodle soup with a stewed beef bone, beef and onion slices
photos.caption: With stewed beef bone (xương bò hầm), one of the extras.

photos.alt: Close-up of beef noodle soup with sliced red chilli and chilli oil on round rice noodles
photos.caption: Round rice noodles, red chilli and a spoon of chilli oil.

photos.alt: Two bowls of beef noodle soup on a steel table with a plate of lime and chilli
photos.caption: Lime and chilli on the side, to adjust the bowl yourself.

photos.alt: Two bowls of beef noodle soup seen from above, one with a slice of chả
photos.caption: Tái, nạm, chả and gân: the normal bowl.

photos.alt: A narrow alley with plastic stools and a small noodle stall under blue awnings
photos.caption: The shop sits in the alley; look for the stools and pots under the awnings.

photos.alt: A yellow sign reading Bún bò Phú Bình with the menu, next to a red stool with a basket of greens
photos.caption: The sign on Lạc Long Quân street.

body: This shop is also in the Phú Bình parish area of old District 11, a few minutes from Hỷ Ký. A bowl costs 50,000 dong and comes with rare beef (tái), brisket (nạm), chả and tendon (gân). You can also add pork knuckle (giò) or stewed beef bones (xương bò hầm).

It is Hue-style bún bò. The broth is clean and gently sweet, with a warm, spicy kick. It doesn't pile on the seasoning the way some places do; some shops add more fermented shrimp paste (mắm ruốc) or season heavily with fish sauce.
That is why I think it suits visitors: if this is your first bún bò, the broth here is a gentle place to start.
The shop sells in the morning only.
Verdict: very worth trying.

Practical info: Bún bò Phú Bình, in alley 423 Lạc Long Quân, Hòa Bình ward (the Phú Bình area of old District 11). The sign out on the street gives the address as 20W Lạc Long Quân. 50,000 dong a bowl. Mornings only.

stories.title: Two old faces of District 11: a Trần Quý shophouse and the Phú Thọ grandstand
stories.dek: A weathered 1960s-style family shophouse and the 1930s racecourse grandstand that may be kept as heritage, a few minutes apart in old District 11.

photos.alt: A weathered white two-storey shophouse with terracotta breeze-block panels, dark louvred shutters, blue folding steel gates and a rooftop terrace, with a street cart of steel pots in front
photos.caption: A family shophouse on Trần Quý Street: breeze blocks, louvres, folding gates and a rooftop that grew over the years. House numbers and signs blurred for privacy.

photos.alt: The long ochre grandstand of the old Phú Thọ racecourse with stepped towers and arched windows, behind green construction hoarding, with motorbikes passing on the road
photos.caption: The old Phú Thọ racecourse grandstand from Lê Đại Hành Street, behind construction hoarding. Number plates and faces blurred.

body: Two buildings I passed on one sunny morning in old District 11, only a few minutes apart. One is an ordinary family house, the other a landmark most of Saigon remembers. Both say a lot about how this part of Cholon was built.

The first is a double-fronted shophouse on Trần Quý Street. It is the kind of house Saigon built in great numbers after the 1950s: a reinforced-concrete frame, flat roof, lime-washed walls and no decoration for its own sake. Everything on the façade is there to deal with the climate.

Look at the panels of terracotta breeze blocks (gạch bông gió) above the ground floor. They let air and light in and keep the hard sun and most of the rain out, so the house can stay cool without air conditioning. Upstairs, dark louvred shutters do the same job. The parapet of the old roof terrace uses a second breeze-block pattern, in concrete rings.

Then come the layers added over the years: a corrugated metal awning over the windows, and on the roof a new storey of steel-pipe railings, tarpaulin and potted plants. Few houses here are ever rebuilt in one go, so a single façade often shows three or four decades at once. The black streaks are simply many rainy seasons on lime paint.

The ground floor is classic shophouse: a folding steel lattice gate and a slatted shutter that open the whole front, so the room can be a shop, a workshop or the family's front room depending on the decade. Next to the door is a small altar to the Earth God, as in most Cholon homes and shops. The morning I passed, a street seller had parked a cart of shining steel pots in front.

The second building is the grandstand of the Phú Thọ racecourse on Lê Đại Hành Street. The Saigon Racing Club bought the land, a former cemetery of more than 40 hectares, in 1932, and racing began in the mid-1930s. By the 1960s the track kept around 200 racehorses. Racing stopped in 1975, came back in 1989 and ended for good in 2011, when the site was turned over to the city's sports training centre.

The grandstand is a long, symmetrical block with stepped towers, flat projecting roof slabs, strong vertical piers and arched openings at street level. It reads as the Art Deco-influenced modern style that was fashionable in the 1930s: solid geometry instead of classical columns. Later additions sit on top of it, like the glass lift shaft and the sports centre's sign with the Olympic rings. The ochre and red paint is peeling, and small plants grow on the central tower.

The area around it is being rebuilt: five new roads through the old track, parks, schools, a circus and performing arts theatre and a renovated Phú Thọ indoor arena. The city's 2018 zoning plan says the existing grandstand is being studied to be kept as a cultural landmark, and press reports from early 2026 describe it still standing and used by the sports centre. Its final use has not been announced yet, so it is worth seeing while it still looks like this.

If you go: both are best seen from the pavement. The racecourse grounds are a construction site and are not open to visitors, and the shophouse is a private home, so please be discreet with your camera. Mornings give the best light on both façades.

stories.title: Đèn Năm Ngọn at night: Saigon's biggest fabric market, asleep
stories.dek: After closing time at the Five-Lamp roundabout, where Soái Kình Lâm, Saigon's largest wholesale fabric market, sits behind rows of teal shutters.

photos.alt: A small roundabout with a lamp post at night in front of a long three-storey market building signed Thương Xá Đồng Khánh, its shutters closed
photos.caption: The little roundabout at Đèn Năm Ngọn, with Thương xá Đồng Khánh behind it. Posters, phone numbers and number plates blurred.

photos.alt: Close-up of the green and red Thương Xá Đồng Khánh sign above closed shutters and striped awnings at night
photos.caption: Thương xá Đồng Khánh, home of the Soái Kình Lâm fabric market. Open in the daytime only.

photos.alt: A quiet street corner at night with bright street lamps, shophouses with awnings and the end of the Đồng Khánh market building
photos.caption: Looking from the corner across Trần Hưng Đạo towards Phùng Hưng.

photos.alt: Old shophouses with arched windows, blue-painted mouldings and wrought-iron balconies above closed shops at night, next to a 1960s-style apartment block
photos.caption: Arched shophouses with iron balconies on Trần Hưng Đạo, next to a later apartment block.

photos.alt: An empty street at night lined with closed shops and awnings, a lit church spire glowing at the far end
photos.caption: Trần Hưng Đạo after closing, with the lit spire of Cha Tam Church at the far end.

body: By nine on a weekday night, the corner of Trần Hưng Đạo and Phùng Hưng in old District 5 is almost empty. The shutters are down, a street sweeper works around the little roundabout, and the only crowd is at a late-night phở and bánh mì stall on the far corner.

Locals still call this corner Đèn Năm Ngọn, "the five lamps". The name comes from a single lamp post that once stood on the roundabout with five lamps: four lighting the four corners of the junction and one pointing up at the sky. The post standing there today is a modern one, but the name has stuck for generations. Before 1975 this stretch of Trần Hưng Đạo was called Đồng Khánh Street, and that old name lives on in shop names around here.

The long building behind the roundabout is Thương xá Đồng Khánh, and its ground floor is the Soái Kình Lâm fabric market. The market took shape in 1989, when the district gathered the area's fabric traders under one roof here. Stallholders say the name comes from Soái Kình Lâm, a large Chinese restaurant that once stood next door. It grew into Saigon's biggest wholesale fabric market, with close to 1,000 stalls in its early years and around 500 in recent reports. Tailors and shops from the city and the Mekong provinces buy their cloth here; the stalls facing Trần Hưng Đạo are known for áo dài fabric.

At night you notice the buildings instead of the bolts of cloth. Next to the market, a row of older shophouses has tall arched windows picked out in blue, ornate pilasters and wrought-iron balconies full of plants, the mixed French and Chinese style that Cholon merchants built in the early twentieth century. Right beside them rises a plain concrete apartment block with long open galleries, a few decades younger. One short block holds a century of the city.

Look straight down Trần Hưng Đạo and the lit spire of Cha Tam Church glows at the end of the street. In the daytime this is one of the busiest stretches of Cholon; at night it feels like a stage set waiting for the morning.

If you go: come in the daytime to see the fabric market itself (stalls open roughly 7:30am to 4:30pm). It is a wholesale market first, so expect busy traders rather than a souvenir shop. Phùng Hưng Market is a few minutes' walk up Phùng Hưng Street, the herbal medicine shops of Hải Thượng Lãn Ông are close by, and Lâm Thạnh is a good place for a bowl of chè afterwards. At night, the corner is quiet and fine to walk, and makes a good photo stop on the way to Cholon's late food stalls.

stories.title: Phở Mai: a neighbourhood bowl of phở near Nguyễn Tri Phương Market
stories.dek: Clear, sweet broth, four cuts of beef and a poached egg on the side, at a no-frills phở shop in the Nhật Tảo area of District 10.

photos.alt: Overhead view of a bowl of beef phở with rare beef, flank, tendon, spring onion, coriander and black pepper, next to a dish of hoisin and chilli sauce
photos.caption: A mixed bowl: tái, nạm, gân and gàu, with spring onion, coriander and black pepper.

photos.alt: The full table from above: a bowl of phở, a poached egg in broth, bean sprouts, sliced chilli and a swirl of hoisin and chilli sauce on a steel table
photos.caption: The full spread on a steel table: phở, poached egg, bean sprouts, fresh chilli and the hoisin–chilli swirl.

photos.alt: Close-up of a bowl of phở with clear broth, slices of beef and lots of spring onion
photos.caption: Clear, fragrant broth.

photos.alt: A small bowl with a poached egg in broth topped with spring onion and pepper, bean sprouts and chopsticks beside it
photos.caption: Trứng chần: an egg poached in hot broth, ordered on the side.

photos.alt: Two bowls of phở, a poached egg, bean sprouts and sliced chilli on a steel table
photos.caption: Two bowls, one egg to share.

body: If you want phở the way locals eat it on an ordinary morning, skip the tourist-heavy spots and head to District 10. Near Nguyễn Tri Phương Market, in the Nhật Tảo area, Phở Mai is a true neighbourhood favourite where people come for a proper bowl and nothing else.
The broth is the reason to come: clear, fragrant and naturally sweet from hours of simmering beef bones and spices. It is not cloudy or heavy, and you can taste the beef before you add anything.

The meat is a generous mix of four cuts: tái (rare beef, cooked by the hot broth at the table), nạm (flank), gân (tendon, soft and gelatinous) and gàu (fatty brisket). Everything is tender and fresh. On top go plenty of spring onion, a little coriander and a sprinkle of black pepper.

On the side you get a plate of bean sprouts, sliced fresh chilli and the classic dish of hoisin and chilli sauce, so you can adjust every spoonful. Locals tend to dip the meat into the sauce rather than squeeze it all into the broth.

The local pro move: order a side of trứng chần, an egg poached in hot broth with spring onion and pepper. Dip the rare beef into the runny yolk. It is simple and rich, and exactly how many people in Saigon like their phở.
Pull up a metal stool at a steel table, watch the neighbourhood go by and enjoy a steaming bowl that feels like real everyday Saigon. No frills, just excellent phở.

If you go: Phở Mai is near Nguyễn Tri Phương Market in the Nhật Tảo area of District 10. Like most phở shops, it is at its best in the morning. Nhật Tảo Market is a short walk away if you want to explore the neighbourhood after breakfast.

stories.title: Riding Saigon's Metro Line 1: Ben Thanh to Thu Duc and back
stories.dek: A real ride on Metro Line 1: buying a ticket at Ben Thanh, what it cost (29,000 dong with deposit), getting the deposit back at Thu Duc, and tips for visitors.

photos.alt: A blue-and-white Metro Line 1 train at an elevated platform with screen doors and a station attendant
photos.caption: Arriving at Thu Duc, one of the elevated stations. Faces blurred.

photos.alt: Stairs leading down from a covered street entrance into Ben Thanh underground station
photos.caption: Into Ben Thanh station from the street.

photos.caption: Every exit is numbered and lists the streets it leads to.

photos.caption: The ticket machines and counter at Ben Thanh.

photos.alt: Long elevated platform at Thu Duc station with screen doors and a curved steel roof
photos.caption: The elevated platform at Thu Duc.

body: Metro Line 1 is the easiest way to get from the city centre out to the east of Saigon without sitting in traffic. I rode it on a Saturday morning in November, from Ben Thanh to Thu Duc and back, and photographed every step so you know exactly what to expect.

Ben Thanh station is underground, right next to Ben Thanh Market. The passages are wide, air-conditioned and well signed in Vietnamese and English, and every exit is numbered with the streets it leads to.

There are three ways to pay. The fastest is to tap a contactless Visa or Mastercard, or scan an e-wallet QR code, straight at the gate. You can also buy a QR ticket at a kiosk by card. The classic ticket machines take cash only.

I used a ticket machine to see how it works. You pick your destination on the line map, and the screen shows the fare. Ben Thanh to Thu Duc was 14,000 dong, plus a 15,000 dong deposit for the plastic card: 29,000 dong in total. The machine takes notes from 1,000 dong up; it did not take bank cards.

Tap the card at the gate and head down to the platform. The trains are clean, cool and quiet, with announcements and screens in English. From tapping in at Ben Thanh to stepping out on the platform at Thu Duc took about 25 minutes, including the wait.

After the underground stretch, the line rises onto a viaduct and the stations are elevated, with long covered platforms and screen doors. Thu Duc is an ordinary neighbourhood station, a good way to see everyday life on the east side of the city.

The tip most visitors miss: keep your single-journey card, because you need it to exit, and then put it back into a ticket machine at your destination using the card return option. The machine gives you your 15,000 dong deposit back in cash.
For the ride back, follow the signs for platform 1 towards Ben Thanh. Rush hours are busy, but on a weekend morning there was plenty of room.

If you go: the line runs from about 5 am to 10 pm on weekdays and until 11 pm at weekends. Have small notes ready if you use the machines, or simply tap a contactless bank card at the gate. Full details on stations, fares and day passes are in the HCMC Insider metro guide.
